Logistic regression is the go-to model for yes/no questions: will a customer churn, is an email spam, will a loan default. It is simple, fast and easy to explain, which is why it remains a strong baseline.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- How the sigmoid turns any score into a probability
- How the model is trained with log-loss
- How to read the decision boundary
:::

## Intuition

A linear model gives a score $z$ that can be any number. We need a probability between 0 and 1. The sigmoid function squashes the score into that range.

## The math

The model computes a linear score and passes it through the sigmoid:

$$
z = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b, \qquad
\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
$$ {#eq-sigmoid}

Training minimises the log-loss (binary cross-entropy):

$$
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, b) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_i \log \hat{p}_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{p}_i)\Big]
$$ {#eq-logloss}

where $\hat{p}_i = \sigma(z_i)$ from @eq-sigmoid.

::: {#def-boundary}
## Decision boundary
The set of points where $\hat{p} = 0.5$, which is exactly where $z = 0$. For two features it is a straight line.
:::

## Try it yourself

Move the slider to change the weight $w$. A larger weight makes the model more confident.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {ms, msStyle} from "/assets/js/ms-plot.js"
viewof w = Inputs.range([0.2, 5], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Steepness w"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
data = d3.range(-8, 8.01, 0.05).map(z => ({z, p: 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-w * z))}))
Plot.plot({
  ...msStyle,
  y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Probability"},
  x: {label: "z"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(data, {x: "z", y: "p", stroke: ms.indigo, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {strokeDasharray: "4,4", strokeOpacity: 0.4})
  ]
})
```

## The sigmoid, interactively

Hover over the curve to read exact probabilities. Drag to zoom and double-click to reset.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sigmoid
#| fig-cap: "The sigmoid maps any score to a probability between 0 and 1."
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG   # also turns on the site theme

z = np.linspace(-8, 8, 300)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=z, y=1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)), mode="lines", name="σ(z)",
                line=dict(color=COLORS["indigo"], width=3),
                hovertemplate="z = %{x:.2f}<br>p = %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>")
fig.add_hline(y=0.5, line_dash="dash", line_color="#8A93A3", opacity=0.6)
fig.update_layout(height=360, xaxis_title="Score z", yaxis_title="Probability",
                  yaxis_range=[-0.03, 1.03], showlegend=False)
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

As @fig-sigmoid shows, large positive scores give probabilities near 1.

## A real classifier

We train a model on two features and colour the plane by predicted probability. Hover any point to see its class.

```{python}
#| label: fig-boundary
#| fig-cap: "Predicted probability across the feature space. The dashed line is the 0.5 decision boundary."
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=300, n_features=2, n_redundant=0,
                           n_clusters_per_class=1, class_sep=1.2, random_state=4)
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)

g1 = np.linspace(X[:, 0].min() - .5, X[:, 0].max() + .5, 150)
g2 = np.linspace(X[:, 1].min() - .5, X[:, 1].max() + .5, 150)
G1, G2 = np.meshgrid(g1, g2)
P = model.predict_proba(np.c_[G1.ravel(), G2.ravel()])[:, 1].reshape(G1.shape)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_contour(x=g1, y=g2, z=P, colorscale=[[0, COLORS["teal"]], [0.5, "rgba(138,147,163,0.08)"], [1, COLORS["indigo"]]],
                opacity=0.45, contours=dict(start=0, end=1, size=0.1), line_width=0,
                colorbar=dict(title="p(y=1)", thickness=12, len=0.8), hoverinfo="skip")
fig.add_contour(x=g1, y=g2, z=P, contours=dict(start=0.5, end=0.5, coloring="none"),
                line=dict(color="#8A93A3", dash="dash", width=2), showscale=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                name="Decision boundary", showlegend=True)
for cls, color, name in [(0, COLORS["teal"], "Class 0"), (1, COLORS["indigo"], "Class 1")]:
    m = y == cls
    fig.add_scatter(x=X[m, 0], y=X[m, 1], mode="markers", name=name,
                    marker=dict(color=color, size=7, line=dict(color="white", width=0.8)))
fig.update_layout(height=440, xaxis_title="Feature 1", yaxis_title="Feature 2")
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

## The code

Training a model takes three lines with scikit-learn:

```{.python filename="train.py"}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

model = LogisticRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
probs = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]      # probability of class 1
```

The same idea in other languages:

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Python
```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
```
## R
```r
glm(churn ~ tenure + spend, data = df, family = binomial)
```
## SQL
```sql
-- Scoring a trained model inside the warehouse
SELECT customer_id,
       1 / (1 + EXP(-(0.8 * tenure - 0.03 * spend + 1.2))) AS churn_probability
FROM customers;
```
:::

## Metrics to report

| Metric | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Accuracy | Share of correct predictions, misleading when classes are imbalanced |
| Precision / Recall | Quality of positive predictions and share of positives found |
| ROC AUC | Ranking quality across all thresholds |
| Log-loss | How well calibrated the probabilities are |

: Common classification metrics {#tbl-metrics}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Always scale features (for example with `StandardScaler`) before fitting with regularisation, otherwise features with large units dominate the penalty.
:::

## Summary

- Logistic regression is a linear score passed through the sigmoid.
- It is trained by minimising log-loss (@eq-logloss).
- The decision boundary is where $z = 0$, a straight line in feature space.

For a rigorous treatment, see @hastie2009.
